reading.body:
Eight applications now speak the Model Context Protocol, with five open-source, creating a foundation for AI agents to integrate external tools and data sources across development environments.

MCP clients cluster heavily in code editing and AI agent tools. Claude's desktop, web, and CLI versions anchor the protocol's adoption as its first client family. Five specialized editors, Cursor, Windsurf, Zed, VS Code, and Continue, have integrated MCP support directly into their agent workflows. Cline and Goose, both open-source, use MCP as their extensibility layer for local agent execution. The concentration in development tools reflects where agents need to operate: integrated with compilers, version control, file systems, and human workflows.

This matters for AI infrastructure because MCP standardizes how agents access resources without centralizing them. An agent running locally can connect to remote servers, APIs, and databases through a common protocol rather than custom integrations. Decentralized tool access reduces the need for agents to move data through a central platform, potentially lowering network load and inference latency.

The data covers only which applications consume MCP servers, not how many servers exist, which tools see the heaviest use, or whether standardization is actually accelerating adoption compared to custom integration. It also does not distinguish between MCP support that is stable and production-ready versus experimental.
